title: Building the Classes
objective: Build a Ship class and an Alien class that can damage each other and report whether they've been destroyed.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: A Ship That Fires Bullets; Aliens! (Project 1: Alien Invasion)
sourceAlignment.note: Original Code Forge capstone inspired by the book's Alien Invasion project's class structure, adapted to a text-based stdout simulation because Code Forge's grading harness cannot run a graphical pygame event loop. All prose and code are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: With ForgeSettings ready, the next step is the objects that actually fight: a Ship and an Alien. Both share a shape — each one has health and an attack power, each one can take damage, and each one can be asked whether it's destroyed.

A take_damage(amount) method should subtract from health, but never let health drop below zero — a ship at -15 HP doesn't mean anything, so clamp it to 0. A separate is_destroyed() method just checks whether health has reached zero, keeping the 'am I dead?' question in one place instead of repeating the comparison everywhere.

Notice that Ship and Alien don't need to inherit from each other here — they just happen to share a similar shape. That's fine. Inheritance is for when one class truly is a specialized version of another, not just because two classes look alike.
explanation.rule: Give every stateful object a method to change its state (take_damage) and a method to ask about its state (is_destroyed) — don't scatter that logic elsewhere.

examples.title: A Damageable Object
examples.note: max(0, ...) stops health from going negative, and is_destroyed() reads cleanly wherever it's used.

checks.question: Why does take_damage() use max(0, self.health - amount) instead of just self.health -= amount?
options: It prevents health from going below zero, which wouldn't make sense for a destroyed object.
It has no real effect — both are the same.

feedback.correct: Correct — clamping keeps health meaningful even after a killing blow.
feedback.incorrect: Try tracing through take_damage(30) on an object with 20 health without the max().

assignment.title: Ship and Alien Classes
assignment.brief: Define a Ship class and an Alien class that can attack and damage each other, then show one exchange of damage.
requirements: Define class Ship with __init__(self, health, attack_power) storing both as attributes.
Define class Alien with __init__(self, health, attack_power) storing both as attributes.
Both classes need take_damage(self, amount) that reduces health but never below 0.
Both classes need is_destroyed(self) returning True when health is 0.

Write a function battle_round(ship, alien) that has the alien damage the ship by alien.attack_power, then has the ship damage the alien by ship.attack_power, then prints 'Ship HP: {ship.health} | Alien HP: {alien.health}'.
Do not use a while loop yet — that's the next lesson.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_ship = Ship(100, 15)
_cf_alien = Alien(20, 10)
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    battle_round(_cf_ship, _cf_alien)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: battle_round(Ship(100,15), Alien(20,10)) prints 'Ship HP: 90 | Alien HP: 5'

hints: Ship and Alien have the identical shape — write one, then reuse its pattern for the other.
take_damage should look like: self.health = max(0, self.health - amount).
is_destroyed just compares self.health to 0 and returns the result.
In battle_round, damage the ship first (alien.attack_power), then the alien (ship.attack_power), then print the line with an f-string.
